raw: CHAPTER XV. Knitting
en: [Chapter 15] Knitting

raw: There had been earlier drinking than usual in the wine-shop of Monsieur Defarge.
en: Drinking began earlier than usual in Monsieur Defarge's wine shop.

raw: As early as six o’clock in the morning, sallow faces peeping through its barred windows had descried other faces within, bending over measures of wine.
en: As early as six o’clock in the morning, pale faces looking through the barred windows could see other customers inside, bending over their wine glasses.

raw: Monsieur Defarge sold a very thin wine at the best of times, but it would seem to have been an unusually thin wine that he sold at this time.
en: Defarge sold a very cheap, thin wine at the best of times, but the wine he served now seemed unusually sour and thin.

raw: A sour wine, moreover, or a souring, for its influence on the mood of those who drank it was to make them gloomy.
en: It had a gloomy effect on the mood of those who drank it.

raw: No vivacious Bacchanalian flame leaped out of the pressed grape of Monsieur Defarge: but, a smouldering fire that burnt in the dark, lay hidden in the dregs of it.
en: No cheerful laughter came from the grapes of Monsieur Defarge; instead, a quiet, smoldering anger lay hidden in the dregs.

raw: This had been the third morning in succession, on which there had been early drinking at the wine-shop of Monsieur Defarge.
en: This was the third morning in a row that early drinking had occurred at the shop, starting on Monday and continuing to Wednesday.

raw: It had begun on Monday, and here was Wednesday come.
en: However, there was more quiet plotting than drinking.

raw: There had been more of early brooding than drinking; for, many men had listened and whispered and slunk about there from the time of the opening of the door, who could not have laid a piece of money on the counter to save their souls.
en: There had been more early brooding than drinking; for many men had been listening, whispering, and sneaking about from the moment the doors opened, even though they couldn't afford to put a single coin on the counter to save their lives.

raw: These were to the full as interested in the place, however, as if they could have commanded whole barrels of wine; and they glided from seat to seat, and from corner to corner, swallowing talk in lieu of drink, with greedy looks.
en: They were just as interested in the place as if they could afford whole barrels, moving from seat to seat, eagerly absorbing every word.

raw: Notwithstanding an unusual flow of company, the master of the wine-shop was not visible.
en: Despite the crowd, the master of the wine shop was nowhere to be seen.

raw: He was not missed; for, nobody who crossed the threshold looked for him, nobody asked for him, nobody wondered to see only Madame Defarge in her seat, presiding over the distribution of wine, with a bowl of battered small coins before her, as much defaced and beaten out of their original impress as the small coinage of humanity from whose ragged pockets they had come.
en: He was not missed, as no one looked or asked for him. Everyone was used to seeing Madame Defarge sitting at the counter alone, presiding over the wine sales. In front of her sat a bowl of worn, battered coins, which were as damaged and defaced as the poor pockets they had come from.

raw: A suspended interest and a prevalent absence of mind, were perhaps observed by the spies who looked in at the wine-shop, as they looked in at every place, high and low, from the king’s palace to the criminal’s gaol.
en: The suspense and widespread distraction were probably noticed by the spies who peeked into the wine shop, just as they spied on every place, high and low, from the king's palace to the criminals' prison.

raw: Games at cards languished, players at dominoes musingly built towers with them, drinkers drew figures on the tables with spilt drops of wine, Madame Defarge herself picked out the pattern on her sleeve with her toothpick, and saw and heard something inaudible and invisible a long way off.
en: Card games were neglected, domino players built towers with their tiles, and drinkers drew shapes on the tables with spilled wine. Madame Defarge herself picked at her sleeve with a toothpick, looking as if she were seeing and hearing things far away.

raw: Thus, Saint Antoine in this vinous feature of his, until midday.
en: This was the state of the Saint Antoine neighborhood until midday.

raw: It was high noontide, when two dusty men passed through his streets and under his swinging lamps: of whom, one was Monsieur Defarge: the other a mender of roads in a blue cap.
en: At noon, two dusty men walked under the street lamps: Monsieur Defarge and a road mender wearing a blue cap.

raw: All adust and athirst, the two entered the wine-shop.
en: Covered in dust and thirsty, they entered the wine shop.

raw: Their arrival had lighted a kind of fire in the breast of Saint Antoine, fast spreading as they came along, which stirred and flickered in flames of faces at most doors and windows.
en: Their arrival caused a stir in Saint Antoine, with faces appearing at doors and windows as they walked by.

raw: Yet, no one had followed them, and no man spoke when they entered the wine-shop, though the eyes of every man there were turned upon them.
en: Yet no one followed them inside, and no one spoke when they entered, though all eyes turned toward them.

raw: “Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.
en: "Good day, gentlemen!" said Monsieur Defarge.

raw: It may have been a signal for loosening the general tongue. It elicited an answering chorus of “Good day!”
en: This signal loosened the tongues in the room, eliciting a chorus of "Good day!"

raw: “It is bad weather, gentlemen,” said Defarge, shaking his head.
en: "It is bad weather, gentlemen," said Defarge, shaking his head.

raw: Upon which, every man looked at his neighbour, and then all cast down their eyes and sat silent.
en: At this, every man looked at his neighbor, then looked down and sat in silence.

raw: Except one man, who got up and went out.
en: One man got up and walked out.

raw: “My wife,” said Defarge aloud, addressing Madame Defarge: “I have travelled certain leagues with this good mender of roads, called Jacques.
en: "My wife," Defarge said aloud, addressing Madame Defarge. "I have traveled some distance with this good road mender, named Jacques.

raw: I met him--by accident--a day and half’s journey out of Paris.
en: I met him by accident a day and a half's journey outside Paris.

raw: He is a good child, this mender of roads, called Jacques.
en: He is a good fellow, this road mender named Jacques.

raw: Give him to drink, my wife!”
en: Give him a drink, wife!"

raw: A second man got up and went out.
en: A second man stood up and left.

raw: Madame Defarge set wine before the mender of roads called Jacques, who doffed his blue cap to the company, and drank.
en: Madame Defarge poured wine for the road mender, who tipped his blue cap to the room and drank.

raw: In the breast of his blouse he carried some coarse dark bread; he ate of this between whiles, and sat munching and drinking near Madame Defarge’s counter.
en: He took some dark bread from his shirt and ate it, sitting near Madame Defarge's counter.

raw: A third man got up and went out.
en: A third man stood up and walked out.

raw: Defarge refreshed himself with a draught of wine--but, he took less than was given to the stranger, as being himself a man to whom it was no rarity--and stood waiting until the countryman had made his breakfast.
en: Defarge drank a glass of wine himself, taking less than the guest, since wine was no luxury to him, and waited for the countryman to finish his breakfast.

raw: He looked at no one present, and no one now looked at him; not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting, and was at work.
en: He looked at no one, and no one looked at him, not even Madame Defarge, who was busy with her knitting.

raw: “Have you finished your repast, friend?” he asked, in due season.
en: "Have you finished your meal, friend?" Defarge asked.

raw: “Yes, thank you.”
en: "Yes, thank you."

raw: “Come, then!
en: "Come then!

raw: You shall see the apartment that I told you you could occupy.
en: I will show you the room I told you about.

raw: It will suit you to a marvel.”
en: It will suit you perfectly."

raw: Out of the wine-shop into the street, out of the street into a courtyard, out of the courtyard up a steep staircase, out of the staircase into a garret--formerly the garret where a white-haired man sat on a low bench, stooping forward and very busy, making shoes.
en: They walked out of the wine shop into the street, through a courtyard, up a dark staircase, and into an attic, the very attic where a white-haired shoemaker had once sat working on his bench.

raw: No white-haired man was there now; but, the three men were there who had gone out of the wine-shop singly.
en: No shoemaker was there now. Instead, the three men who had left the wine shop one by one were waiting.

raw: And between them and the white-haired man afar off, was the one small link, that they had once looked in at him through the chinks in the wall.
en: They and the white-haired man were connected by one thing: they had all looked at him through the cracks in the attic wall.

raw: Defarge closed the door carefully, and spoke in a subdued voice:
en: Defarge closed the door carefully and spoke quietly:

raw: “Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three!
en: "Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three!

raw: This is the witness encountered by appointment, by me, Jacques Four.
en: This is the witness I met by agreement, I, Jacques Four.

raw: He will tell you all.
en: He will tell you everything.

raw: Speak, Jacques Five!”
en: Speak, Jacques Five!"

raw: The mender of roads, blue cap in hand, wiped his swarthy forehead with it, and said, “Where shall I commence, monsieur?”
en: The road mender stood there, blue cap in hand. He wiped his forehead and said, "Where should I start, monsieur?"

raw: “Commence,” was Monsieur Defarge’s not unreasonable reply, “at the commencement.”
en: "Start at the beginning," Defarge replied.

raw: “I saw him then, messieurs,” began the mender of roads, “a year ago this running summer, underneath the carriage of the Marquis, hanging by the chain.
en: "I saw him, messieurs," began the road mender. "It was a year ago during the summer. He was hanging by the chain under the Marquis's carriage.

raw: Behold the manner of it.
en: It happened like this: I had stopped working on the road at sunset.

raw: I leaving my work on the road, the sun going to bed, the carriage of the Marquis slowly ascending the hill, he hanging by the chain--like this.”
en: The Marquis's carriage was slowly climbing the hill. And there he was, hanging by the chain, like this."

raw: Again the mender of roads went through the whole performance; in which he ought to have been perfect by that time, seeing that it had been the infallible resource and indispensable entertainment of his village during a whole year.
en: The road mender acted out the scene again. He was very good at it, since it had been the main story in his village for a whole year.

raw: Jacques One struck in, and asked if he had ever seen the man before?
en: Jacques One asked if he had ever seen the man before.

raw: “Never,” answered the mender of roads, recovering his perpendicular.
en: "Never," answered the road mender.

raw: Jacques Three demanded how he afterwards recognised him then?
en: Jacques Three asked how he recognized him later.

raw: “By his tall figure,” said the mender of roads, softly, and with his finger at his nose. “When Monsieur the Marquis demands that evening, ‘Say, what is he like?’ I make response, ‘Tall as a spectre.’”
en: "By his height," the road mender whispered, putting his finger to his nose. "When the Marquis asked me that evening, 'What does he look like?' I answered, 'Tall as a ghost.'"

raw: “You should have said, short as a dwarf,” returned Jacques Two.
en: "You should have said short as a dwarf," Jacques Two remarked.

raw: “But what did I know?
en: "But how was I to know?

raw: The deed was not then accomplished, neither did he confide in me. Observe!
en: The deed had not been done yet, and he had not told me anything.

raw: Under those circumstances even, I do not offer my testimony.
en: Even then, I did not volunteer to speak.

raw: Monsieur the Marquis indicates me with his finger, standing near our little fountain, and says, ‘To me!
en: The Marquis pointed his finger at me by the fountain and ordered his men to bring me to him.

raw: Bring that rascal!’ My faith, messieurs, I offer nothing.”
en: I had no choice, messieurs."

raw: “He is right there, Jacques,” murmured Defarge, to him who had interrupted. “Go on!”
en: "He is right," Defarge muttered to the man who had interrupted. "Go on!"

raw: “Good!” said the mender of roads, with an air of mystery. “The tall man is lost, and he is sought--how many months?
en: "Good!" said the road mender. "The tall man disappeared, and they searched for him for months.

raw: Nine, ten, eleven?”
en: Was it nine, ten, eleven months?"

raw: “No matter, the number,” said Defarge. “He is well hidden, but at last he is unluckily found.
en: "It doesn't matter how long," said Defarge. "He hid well, but at last they found him.

raw: Go on!”
en: Go on!"

raw: “I am again at work upon the hill-side, and the sun is again about to go to bed.
en: "I was working on the hillside again at sunset.

raw: I am collecting my tools to descend to my cottage down in the village below, where it is already dark, when I raise my eyes, and see coming over the hill six soldiers.
en: I was gathering my tools to go home, where it was already dark, when I looked up and saw six soldiers coming over the hill.

raw: In the midst of them is a tall man with his arms bound--tied to his sides--like this!”
en: In the middle of them was the tall man, his arms tied to his sides, like this!"

raw: With the aid of his indispensable cap, he represented a man with his elbows bound fast at his hips, with cords that were knotted behind him.
en: Using his blue cap, he showed how the man's elbows were tied tightly behind him with knotted ropes.

raw: “I stand aside, messieurs, by my heap of stones, to see the soldiers and their prisoner pass (for it is a solitary road, that, where any spectacle is well worth looking at), and at first, as they approach, I see no more than that they are six soldiers with a tall man bound, and that they are almost black to my sight--except on the side of the sun going to bed, where they have a red edge, messieurs.
en: "I stood by my heap of stones to watch them pass, as it is a quiet road where any spectacle is worth watching. At first, as they approached, I only saw six soldiers and the bound man. They looked black against the setting sun, which gave them a red edge, messieurs.

raw: Also, I see that their long shadows are on the hollow ridge on the opposite side of the road, and are on the hill above it, and are like the shadows of giants.
en: Their long shadows stretched like giants across the hill. They were covered in dust, marching tramp, tramp!

raw: Also, I see that they are covered with dust, and that the dust moves with them as they come, tramp, tramp!
en: But when they came close, I recognized the tall man, and he recognized me.

raw: But when they advance quite near to me, I recognise the tall man, and he recognises me.
en: But when they got very close to me, I recognized the tall man, and he recognized me.

raw: Ah, but he would be well content to precipitate himself over the hill-side once again, as on the evening when he and I first encountered, close to the same spot!”
en: He would have gladly thrown himself over the hillside again, as he did the first night we met near that very spot!"

raw: He described it as if he were there, and it was evident that he saw it vividly; perhaps he had not seen much in his life.
en: He described it as if he were actually there, and it was obvious that he pictured it vividly; perhaps he hadn't seen much else in his life.

raw: “I do not show the soldiers that I recognise the tall man; he does not show the soldiers that he recognises me; we do it, and we know it, with our eyes. ‘Come on!’ says the chief of that company, pointing to the village, ‘bring him fast to his tomb!’ and they bring him faster.
en: "I did not show the soldiers that I knew him, and he did not show them that he knew me. We spoke only with our eyes. 'Come on!' the sergeant said, pointing toward the village. 'Bring him to his grave!' and they marched faster.

raw: I follow.
en: I followed them.

raw: His arms are swelled because of being bound so tight, his wooden shoes are large and clumsy, and he is lame.
en: His arms were swollen from the tight ropes, his wooden shoes were clumsy, and he was limping.

raw: Because he is lame, and consequently slow, they drive him with their guns--like this!”
en: Because he was slow, the soldiers hit him with their gunstocks, like this!"

raw: He imitated the action of a man’s being impelled forward by the butt-ends of muskets.
en: He acted out a man being pushed forward by musket butts.

raw: “As they descend the hill like madmen running a race, he falls.
en: "As they ran down the hill like madmen, he fell.

raw: They laugh and pick him up again.
en: They laughed and pulled him up.

raw: His face is bleeding and covered with dust, but he cannot touch it; thereupon they laugh again.
en: His face was bleeding and dusty, but he couldn't wipe it because his hands were tied.

raw: They bring him into the village; all the village runs to look; they take him past the mill, and up to the prison; all the village sees the prison gate open in the darkness of the night, and swallow him--like this!”
en: The soldiers laughed again. They brought him into the village, and everyone ran to see. They took him past the mill and up to the prison. Everyone saw the prison gates open in the dark and swallow him up, like this!"

raw: He opened his mouth as wide as he could, and shut it with a sounding snap of his teeth.
en: He opened his mouth wide and snapped his teeth shut.

raw: Observant of his unwillingness to mar the effect by opening it again, Defarge said, “Go on, Jacques.”
en: Seeing he wanted to keep his mouth closed for effect, Defarge said, "Go on, Jacques."

raw: “All the village,” pursued the mender of roads, on tiptoe and in a low voice, “withdraws; all the village whispers by the fountain; all the village sleeps; all the village dreams of that unhappy one, within the locks and bars of the prison on the crag, and never to come out of it, except to perish.
en: "All the villagers went home," the road mender whispered on tiptoe. "Everyone whispered by the fountain, then went to sleep and dreamed of that poor man locked in the prison on the cliff, never to come out alive.

raw: In the morning, with my tools upon my shoulder, eating my morsel of black bread as I go, I make a circuit by the prison, on my way to my work.
en: In the morning, with my tools on my shoulder, eating my bread, I walked past the prison.

raw: There I see him, high up, behind the bars of a lofty iron cage, bloody and dusty as last night, looking through.
en: I saw him high up, behind the iron bars of a cage, still bloody and dusty, looking out.

raw: He has no hand free, to wave to me; I dare not call to him; he regards me like a dead man.”
en: He could not wave because his hands were tied. I did not dare call out to him. He looked at me like a dead man."

raw: Defarge and the three glanced darkly at one another.
en: Defarge and the other three men looked at one another with dark, vengeful expressions.

raw: The looks of all of them were dark, repressed, and revengeful, as they listened to the countryman’s story; the manner of all of them, while it was secret, was authoritative too.
en: All their expressions were dark, restrained, and vengeful as they listened to the countryman's story. While their behavior was secretive, it was also authoritative.

raw: They had the air of a rough tribunal; Jacques One and Two sitting on the old pallet-bed, each with his chin resting on his hand, and his eyes intent on the road-mender; Jacques Three, equally intent, on one knee behind them, with his agitated hand always gliding over the network of fine nerves about his mouth and nose; Defarge standing between them and the narrator, whom he had stationed in the light of the window, by turns looking from him to them, and from them to him.
en: They looked like a rough jury. Jacques One and Two sat on the old straw bed, each with his chin resting on his hand, staring intently at the road-mender. Jacques Three was equally focused, resting on one knee behind them with his nervous hand constantly rubbing the fine nerves around his mouth and nose. Defarge stood between them and the storyteller, whom he had placed in the light of the window, looking back and forth from him to them.

raw: “Go on, Jacques,” said Defarge.
en: "Go on, Jacques," Defarge said.

raw: “He remains up there in his iron cage some days.
en: "He stayed in that iron cage for several days.

raw: The village looks at him by stealth, for it is afraid.
en: The villagers watched him secretly, fearing the soldiers.

raw: But it always looks up, from a distance, at the prison on the crag; and in the evening, when the work of the day is achieved and it assembles to gossip at the fountain, all faces are turned towards the prison.
en: But the whole village always looked up from a distance at the prison on the cliff. In the evening, when the day's work was done and everyone gathered to gossip at the fountain, all faces were turned toward the prison.

raw: Formerly, they were turned towards the posting-house; now, they are turned towards the prison.
en: In the evening, when they gathered by the fountain, all faces turned toward the prison instead of the post house.

raw: They whisper at the fountain, that although condemned to death he will not be executed; they say that petitions have been presented in Paris, showing that he was enraged and made mad by the death of his child; they say that a petition has been presented to the King himself.
en: They whispered at the fountain that even though he was sentenced to death, he wouldn't be executed. People said that petitions were presented in Paris, explaining that he was enraged and driven mad by the death of his child, and even that a petition was given to the King himself.

raw: What do I know?
en: They said petitions had been sent to Paris, explaining that he had gone mad from the death of his child, and that a petition had been given to the King himself.

raw: It is possible.
en: I don't know if it's true.

raw: Perhaps yes, perhaps no.”
en: Perhaps yes, perhaps no."

raw: “Listen then, Jacques,” Number One of that name sternly interposed. “Know that a petition was presented to the King and Queen.
en: "Listen, Jacques," Jacques One said sternly. "A petition was indeed given to the King and Queen.

raw: All here, yourself excepted, saw the King take it, in his carriage in the street, sitting beside the Queen.
en: Everyone here, except you, saw the King take it from his carriage in the street.

raw: It is Defarge whom you see here, who, at the hazard of his life, darted out before the horses, with the petition in his hand.”
en: It was Defarge who ran out before the horses at the risk of his life to hand it to him."

raw: “And once again listen, Jacques!” said the kneeling Number Three: his fingers ever wandering over and over those fine nerves, with a strikingly greedy air, as if he hungered for something--that was neither food nor drink; “the guard, horse and foot, surrounded the petitioner, and struck him blows.
en: "And listen once again, Jacques!" said the kneeling Number Three, his fingers constantly rubbing his nervous face with a strangely greedy look, as if he hungered for something that wasn't food or drink. "The guards on horseback and on foot surrounded the petitioner and beat him."

raw: You hear?”
en: Do you hear?"

raw: “I hear, messieurs.”
en: "I hear, messieurs."

raw: “Go on then,” said Defarge.
en: "Go on then," said Defarge.

raw: “Again; on the other hand, they whisper at the fountain,” resumed the countryman, “that he is brought down into our country to be executed on the spot, and that he will very certainly be executed.
en: The road mender continued, "But on the other hand, they whisper by the fountain that he will be executed in our village.

raw: They even whisper that because he has slain Monseigneur, and because Monseigneur was the father of his tenants--serfs--what you will--he will be executed as a parricide.
en: They say that because he killed the Marquis, who was the lord of the land, he will be executed as a parent-killer.

raw: One old man says at the fountain, that his right hand, armed with the knife, will be burnt off before his face; that, into wounds which will be made in his arms, his breast, and his legs, there will be poured boiling oil, melted lead, hot resin, wax, and sulphur; finally, that he will be torn limb from limb by four strong horses.
en: One old man at the fountain said that his right hand, holding the knife, would be burned off right in front of him. He said they would cut his arms, chest, and legs, and pour boiling oil, melted lead, hot resin, wax, and sulfur into the wounds, and finally, he would be torn apart limb by limb by four strong horses.

raw: That old man says, all this was actually done to a prisoner who made an attempt on the life of the late King, Louis Fifteen.
en: They will pour boiling oil, melted lead, and sulfur into his wounds, and then tear him apart with four horses.

raw: But how do I know if he lies?
en: The old man said this was done to Damiens, the man who tried to kill King Louis XV.

raw: I am not a scholar.”
en: But I don't know if it's true; I am not educated."

raw: “Listen once again then, Jacques!” said the man with the restless hand and the craving air. “The name of that prisoner was Damiens, and it was all done in open day, in the open streets of this city of Paris; and nothing was more noticed in the vast concourse that saw it done, than the crowd of ladies of quality and fashion, who were full of eager attention to the last--to the last, Jacques, prolonged until nightfall, when he had lost two legs and an arm, and still breathed!
en: "Listen, Jacques!" the nervous Jacques Three said. "The man was named Damiens, and it was done in broad daylight in the streets of Paris. The wealthy ladies of the court watched the execution until nightfall, when the man was still breathing after losing his limbs!

raw: And it was done--why, how old are you?”
en: It happened when you were ten years old; you could have seen it."

raw: “Thirty-five,” said the mender of roads, who looked sixty. “It was done when you were more than ten years old; you might have seen it.”
en: "Thirty-five," said the road-mender, who looked sixty. "It happened when you were more than ten years old; you might have seen it."

raw: “Enough!” said Defarge, with grim impatience. “Long live the Devil!
en: "Well, some say this and some say that.

raw: Go on.” “Well!
en: On Sunday night, when the village was asleep, the soldiers came down from the prison.

raw: Some whisper this, some whisper that; they speak of nothing else; even the fountain appears to fall to that tune.
en: Some whispered this, some whispered that; they talked of nothing else, and even the fountain seemed to splash to that tune.

raw: At length, on Sunday night when all the village is asleep, come soldiers, winding down from the prison, and their guns ring on the stones of the little street.
en: Finally, on Sunday night when the whole village was asleep, soldiers came marching down from the prison, their guns ringing on the stones of the little street.

raw: Workmen dig, workmen hammer, soldiers laugh and sing; in the morning, by the fountain, there is raised a gallows forty feet high, poisoning the water.”
en: In the morning, a gallows forty feet high was standing by the fountain, shadowing the water."

raw: The mender of roads looked _through_ rather than _at_ the low ceiling, and pointed as if he saw the gallows somewhere in the sky.
en: The road mender pointed toward the ceiling as if he could see the gallows in the sky.

raw: “All work is stopped, all assemble there, nobody leads the cows out, the cows are there with the rest.
en: "All work stopped, and everyone gathered there, even the cows.

raw: At midday, the roll of drums.
en: At noon, the drums rolled.

raw: Soldiers have marched into the prison in the night, and he is in the midst of many soldiers.
en: The soldiers brought him out, bound and gagged with a tight string, making him look like he was laughing." The road mender pulled his mouth back with his thumbs to show them.

raw: He is bound as before, and in his mouth there is a gag--tied so, with a tight string, making him look almost as if he laughed.” He suggested it, by creasing his face with his two thumbs, from the corners of his mouth to his ears. “On the top of the gallows is fixed the knife, blade upwards, with its point in the air.
en: He was tied up as before, and there was a gag in his mouth, tied with a tight string that made him look almost as if he was laughing." He demonstrated this by stretching his mouth to his ears with his thumbs. "At the top of the gallows, they fixed the knife with the blade facing upwards and the point in the air.

raw: He is hanged there forty feet high--and is left hanging, poisoning the water.”
en: He was hanged forty feet in the air, left hanging to poison the water."

raw: They looked at one another, as he used his blue cap to wipe his face, on which the perspiration had started afresh while he recalled the spectacle.
en: They looked at one another in silence as the road mender wiped his sweaty face with his blue cap.

raw: “It is frightful, messieurs.
en: "It is terrible, messieurs.

raw: How can the women and the children draw water!
en: How can the women draw water now?

raw: Who can gossip of an evening, under that shadow! Under it, have I said?
en: Who can sit by the fountain under that shadow?

raw: When I left the village, Monday evening as the sun was going to bed, and looked back from the hill, the shadow struck across the church, across the mill, across the prison--seemed to strike across the earth, messieurs, to where the sky rests upon it!”
en: When I left the village on Monday evening and looked back from the hill, the shadow of the gallows stretched across the church, the mill, the prison, across the whole earth!"

raw: The hungry man gnawed one of his fingers as he looked at the other three, and his finger quivered with the craving that was on him.
en: The hungry man gnawed on one of his fingers as he looked at the other three, and his finger shook with the intense craving he felt.

raw: “That’s all, messieurs.
en: "That is all, messieurs.

raw: I left at sunset (as I had been warned to do), and I walked on, that night and half next day, until I met (as I was warned I should) this comrade.
en: I left at sunset as I was told, walked all night and half the next day, until I met this comrade.

raw: With him, I came on, now riding and now walking, through the rest of yesterday and through last night. And here you see me!”
en: I traveled with him, sometimes riding and sometimes walking, through the rest of yesterday and through last night. And now here you see me!"

raw: After a gloomy silence, the first Jacques said, “Good!
en: After a quiet pause, Jacques One said, "Good!

raw: You have acted and recounted faithfully.
en: You have told your story well.

raw: Will you wait for us a little, outside the door?”
en: Wait for us outside the door."

raw: “Very willingly,” said the mender of roads.
en: "Gladly," said the road mender.

raw: Whom Defarge escorted to the top of the stairs, and, leaving seated there, returned.
en: Defarge led him to the stairs and returned to the attic.

raw: The three had risen, and their heads were together when he came back to the garret.
en: The three men stood with their heads together.

raw: “How say you, Jacques?” demanded Number One. “To be registered?”
en: "What do you say, Jacques?" Number One asked. "Should they be registered?"

raw: “To be registered, as doomed to destruction,” returned Defarge.
en: "To be registered for destruction," Defarge replied.

raw: “Magnificent!” croaked the man with the craving.
en: "Excellent!" Jacques Three croaked.

raw: “The chateau, and all the race?” inquired the first.
en: "The castle and the whole family?" the first asked.

raw: “The chateau and all the race,” returned Defarge. “Extermination.”
en: "The castle and the whole family," Defarge answered. "Extermination."

raw: The hungry man repeated, in a rapturous croak, “Magnificent!” and began gnawing another finger.
en: Jacques Three croaked happily, "Excellent!" and chewed on another finger.

raw: “Are you sure,” asked Jacques Two, of Defarge, “that no embarrassment can arise from our manner of keeping the register?
en: Jacques Two asked Defarge, "Are you sure that there is no danger in how we keep the record?

raw: Without doubt it is safe, for no one beyond ourselves can decipher it; but shall we always be able to decipher it--or, I ought to say, will she?”
en: It is safe because no one else can read it, but will we always be able to read it, or rather, will she?"

raw: “Jacques,” returned Defarge, drawing himself up, “if madame my wife undertook to keep the register in her memory alone, she would not lose a word of it--not a syllable of it.
en: Defarge said proudly, "Jacques, if my wife kept the record in her head alone, she would never lose a word of it.

raw: Knitted, in her own stitches and her own symbols, it will always be as plain to her as the sun.
en: Knitted into her own stitches and symbols, it will always be clear to her.

raw: Confide in Madame Defarge.
en: Trust Madame Defarge.

raw: It would be easier for the weakest poltroon that lives, to erase himself from existence, than to erase one letter of his name or crimes from the knitted register of Madame Defarge.”
en: It would be easier for a man to erase himself from existence than to erase a single letter from her knitted register."

raw: There was a murmur of confidence and approval, and then the man who hungered, asked: “Is this rustic to be sent back soon? I hope so.
en: They murmured in agreement, and Jacques Three asked, "Should we send the countryman back soon?

raw: He is very simple; is he not a little dangerous?”
en: He is very simple; is he dangerous?"

raw: “He knows nothing,” said Defarge; “at least nothing more than would easily elevate himself to a gallows of the same height.
en: "He knows nothing," said Defarge. "Only enough to get himself hanged if he talks.

raw: I charge myself with him; let him remain with me; I will take care of him, and set him on his road.
en: I will take care of him and set him on his way.

raw: He wishes to see the fine world--the King, the Queen, and Court; let him see them on Sunday.”
en: He wants to see the King, Queen, and court. I will take him to Versailles on Sunday."

raw: “What?” exclaimed the hungry man, staring. “Is it a good sign, that he wishes to see Royalty and Nobility?”
en: "What?" Jacques Three asked in surprise. "Is it a good sign that he wants to see royalty?"

raw: “Jacques,” said Defarge; “judiciously show a cat milk, if you wish her to thirst for it.
en: Defarge explained, "Jacques, if you want a cat to catch mice, show her milk first.

raw: Judiciously show a dog his natural prey, if you wish him to bring it down one day.”
en: Show a dog his prey if you want him to hunt it down one day."

raw: Nothing more was said, and the mender of roads, being found already dozing on the topmost stair, was advised to lay himself down on the pallet-bed and take some rest.
en: Nothing more was said. They found the road mender asleep on the stairs and told him to rest on the bed.

raw: He needed no persuasion, and was soon asleep.
en: He fell asleep immediately.

raw: Worse quarters than Defarge’s wine-shop, could easily have been found in Paris for a provincial slave of that degree.
en: For a poor peasant, Defarge’s shop was a comfortable place to stay.

raw: Saving for a mysterious dread of madame by which he was constantly haunted, his life was very new and agreeable.
en: Aside from his fear of Madame Defarge, his time in Paris was very pleasant.

raw: But, madame sat all day at her counter, so expressly unconscious of him, and so particularly determined not to perceive that his being there had any connection with anything below the surface, that he shook in his wooden shoes whenever his eye lighted on her.
en: Madame sat at her counter all day, acting as if he weren't there, which made him shake in his wooden shoes whenever she looked at him.

raw: For, he contended with himself that it was impossible to foresee what that lady might pretend next; and he felt assured that if she should take it into her brightly ornamented head to pretend that she had seen him do a murder and afterwards flay the victim, she would infallibly go through with it until the play was played out.
en: He argued with himself that it was impossible to predict what that lady might pretend next. He was absolutely sure that if she took it into her brightly decorated head to pretend she had seen him commit a murder and then skin the victim, she would completely commit to the act until the very end.

raw: Therefore, when Sunday came, the mender of roads was not enchanted (though he said he was) to find that madame was to accompany monsieur and himself to Versailles.
en: Therefore, when Sunday came, the road mender pretended to be happy to go to Versailles with the Defarges.

raw: It was additionally disconcerting to have madame knitting all the way there, in a public conveyance; it was additionally disconcerting yet, to have madame in the crowd in the afternoon, still with her knitting in her hands as the crowd waited to see the carriage of the King and Queen.
en: It was uncomfortable to have madame knitting in the public carriage all the way, and even more uncomfortable to have her knitting in the crowd as they waited to see the King and Queen.

raw: “You work hard, madame,” said a man near her.
en: "You work hard, madame," a man nearby remarked.

raw: “Yes,” answered Madame Defarge; “I have a good deal to do.”
en: "Yes," Madame Defarge replied. "I have a lot to do."

raw: “What do you make, madame?”
en: "What are you making?"

raw: “Many things.”
en: "Many things."

raw: “For instance--”
en: "For example?"

raw: “For instance,” returned Madame Defarge, composedly, “shrouds.”
en: She replied calmly, "For example, shrouds."

raw: The man moved a little further away, as soon as he could, and the mender of roads fanned himself with his blue cap: feeling it mightily close and oppressive.
en: The man moved away quickly, and the road mender fanned himself with his cap, feeling the heat.

raw: If he needed a King and Queen to restore him, he was fortunate in having his remedy at hand; for, soon the large-faced King and the fair-faced Queen came in their golden coach, attended by the shining Bull’s Eye of their Court, a glittering multitude of laughing ladies and fine lords; and in jewels and silks and powder and splendour and elegantly spurning figures and handsomely disdainful faces of both sexes, the mender of roads bathed himself, so much to his temporary intoxication, that he cried Long live the King, Long live the Queen, Long live everybody and everything! as if he had never heard of ubiquitous Jacques in his time.
en: If he needed a King and Queen to recover, he was lucky to have his cure nearby. Soon, the large-faced King and the fair-faced Queen arrived in their golden coach, accompanied by the shining stars of their Court—a glittering crowd of laughing ladies and elegant lords. The road-mender soaked in the jewels, silks, powder, splendor, and the gracefully snobby figures and handsome, arrogant faces of both sexes. He became so temporarily intoxicated by it all that he shouted, "Long live the King, long live the Queen, long live everybody and everything!" as if he had never even heard of the mysterious Jacques.

raw: Then, there were gardens, courtyards, terraces, fountains, green banks, more King and Queen, more Bull’s Eye, more lords and ladies, more Long live they all! until he absolutely wept with sentiment.
en: Then there were gardens, courtyards, terraces, fountains, green banks, more of the King and Queen, more shining courtiers, more lords and ladies, and more shouts of "Long live them all!" until he literally cried with emotion.

raw: During the whole of this scene, which lasted some three hours, he had plenty of shouting and weeping and sentimental company, and throughout Defarge held him by the collar, as if to restrain him from flying at the objects of his brief devotion and tearing them to pieces.
en: During the three hours of the display, he shouted and cried with the crowd. Defarge held him by the collar the whole time, keeping him from getting too close to the carriage.

raw: “Bravo!” said Defarge, clapping him on the back when it was over, like a patron; “you are a good boy!”
en: "Well done!" Defarge said, clapping him on the back afterward. "You are a good boy!"

raw: The mender of roads was now coming to himself, and was mistrustful of having made a mistake in his late demonstrations; but no.
en: The road mender began to worry if he had made a mistake by cheering the King.

raw: “You are the fellow we want,” said Defarge, in his ear; “you make these fools believe that it will last for ever.
en: "You are exactly the kind of man we need," Defarge whispered. "You make these fools believe their system will last forever.

raw: Then, they are the more insolent, and it is the nearer ended.”
en: That makes them more insolent, and brings the end closer."

raw: “Hey!” cried the mender of roads, reflectively; “that’s true.”
en: "Ah!" said the road mender. "That is true."

raw: “These fools know nothing.
en: "These fools know nothing.

raw: While they despise your breath, and would stop it for ever and ever, in you or in a hundred like you rather than in one of their own horses or dogs, they only know what your breath tells them.
en: They despise you and would kill you before they killed one of their horses, but they only believe what they see.

raw: Let it deceive them, then, a little longer; it cannot deceive them too much.”
en: Let them be deceived a little longer."

raw: Madame Defarge looked superciliously at the client, and nodded in confirmation.
en: Madame Defarge looked at him and nodded.

raw: “As to you,” said she, “you would shout and shed tears for anything, if it made a show and a noise.
en: She said, "As for you, you would cheer for anything that makes a noise.

raw: Say! Would you not?”
en: Wouldn't you?"

raw: “Truly, madame, I think so.
en: "Yes, madame.

raw: For the moment.”
en: For the moment."

raw: “If you were shown a great heap of dolls, and were set upon them to pluck them to pieces and despoil them for your own advantage, you would pick out the richest and gayest. Say! Would you not?”
en: "If you were shown a pile of dolls and told to tear them to pieces for your own profit, you would choose the finest ones, wouldn't you?"

raw: “Truly yes, madame.”
en: "Yes, madame."

raw: “Yes. And if you were shown a flock of birds, unable to fly, and were set upon them to strip them of their feathers for your own advantage, you would set upon the birds of the finest feathers; would you not?”
en: "And if you were shown a flock of fine birds unable to fly and told to pluck their feathers, you would choose the best ones, wouldn't you?"

raw: “It is true, madame.”
en: "That is true, madame."

raw: “You have seen both dolls and birds to-day,” said Madame Defarge, with a wave of her hand towards the place where they had last been apparent; “now, go home!”
en: "You have seen both dolls and birds today," Madame Defarge said, pointing toward the palace. "Now, go home!"
